newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan trade surplus up for first time in two years.
newsitem.headline: Japan trade surplus up for first time in two years.

text.p: Japan's customs-cleared trade surplus rose last month for the first time in over two years, swelling by 6.5 percent from a year earlier to 686.72 billion yen ($5.53 billion), the Finance Ministry said on Monday.

The trade surplus with the United States, often a source of trade friction, also rose in February, growing by 12.3 percent to 407.35 billion yen ($3.28 billion). The figures were not adjusted for seasonal factors.
The rise in the overall surplus was the first since November 1994 and economists said the relatively weaker yen was behind the shift in the trade balance.
Many economists had been expecting the surplus to rise as the recent fall in the value of the yen has accelerated Japan's exports while putting a brake on imports.

"We should be seeing from now on the Japanese surplus starting to pick up fairly steadily and starting to contribute positively to Japanese growth instead of negatively as it has done for the past three years," said Jason James, a strategist at HSBC James Capel.

A Finance Ministry official cited higher export growth as a factor in the trade figures. He said exports had been posting double-digit growth recently although growth in imports continued to exceed growth in exports in value terms.

Car exports were brisk due to a rebound from low levels a year earlier, and demand for cars in the United States should remain strong, he said. The outlook for exports of semiconductor parts to the United States is also bright due to strong demand there for a new type of micro-processing unit, the official said.

In recent months the United States has voiced concern that Japan's trade surplus was about to begin climbing again, calling on the Japanese government to encourage recovery led by domestic demand rather than relying on exports to solve its economic problems.
Economists said a rising surplus should work to push the yen higher over the coming months, as Japanese exporters need to convert more overseas export earnings into yen.

"This should start to exert upward pressure on the yen as awareness grows that the surplus is rising again. I think we have seen the peak in the exchange rate for the moment in terms of dollar strength," said ING Barings economist Richard Jerram. ($1=124 yen)
